source_text:
Ἐπιμένοντος δὲ πάλιν αὐτοῦ καὶ λέγοντος: Ὄμοσον τὴν Καίσαρος τύχην, ἀπεκρίνατο: Εἰ κενοδοξεῖς, ἵνα ὀμόσω τὴν καίσαρος τύχην, ὡς σὺ λέγεις, προσποιεῖ δὲ ἀγνοεῖν με, τίς εἰμι, μετὰ παρρησίας ἄκουε: Χριστιανός εἰμι. εἰ δὲ θέλεις τὸν τοῦ Χριστιανισμοῦ μαθεῖν λόγον, δὸς ἡμέραν καὶ ἄκουσον.
ἔφη ὁ ἀνθύπατος: Πεῖσον τὸν δῆμον. ὁ δὲ Πολύκαρπος εἶπεν: Σὲ μὲν κἂν λόγου ἠξίωσα: δεδιδάγμεθα γὰρ ἀρχαῖς καὶ ἐξουσίαις ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ τεταγμέναις τιμὴν κατὰ τὸ προσῆκον, τὴν μὴ βλάπτουσαν ἡμᾶς, ἀπονέμειν: ἐκείνους δὲ οὐχ ἡγοῦμαι ἀξίους τοῦ ἀπολογεῖσθαι αὐτοῖς.
thought_title: Polycarp's Confession and Refusal to Persuade the Crowd
orientation: Polycarp is being interrogated by the proconsul in the stadium, who has just demanded that he swear by Caesar's fortune and revile Christ.
pass_a_gloss: And [with] him again insisting and saying: Swear the fortune of Caesar, he answered: If you vainly imagine that I will swear the fortune of Caesar, as you say, and you pretend not to know me, who I am, with boldness hear: A Christian I am. And if you wish the word of Christianity to learn, give a day and hear. The proconsul said: Persuade the people. And Polycarp said: You indeed I would have deemed worthy of a word: for we have been taught to authorities and powers by God appointed honor according to what is fitting, the [honor] not harming us, to render: but those I do not consider worthy to make a defense to them.

choices.why: The verb means to have empty or vain opinion; rendering as 'vainly imagine' captures the sense of a false assumption without importing a modern idiom.

choices.english: and you pretend not to know me
choices.why: The verb προσποιέω with infinitive means to pretend or feign; the clause is an accusation that the proconsul is feigning ignorance.
rejected: you make as if to be ignorant of me

choices.why: παρρησία is the frank, bold speech of a free person; rendering as 'boldness' preserves the term's force in a martyrdom context.

choices.english: to learn the word of Christianity
choices.why: λόγος here means the teaching or account; 'word' keeps the literal sense while 'of Christianity' renders the abstract noun.

choices.english: You indeed I would have deemed worthy of a word
choices.why: The aorist with κἄν expresses a past potential; the sense is that Polycarp would have considered the proconsul worthy of a reasoned reply.
rejected: You I would have considered worthy of an account
You at least I would have judged worthy of speech

choices.why: The participle modifies the implied honor; the negative participle specifies that the honor rendered must not harm Christians.

bible_refs.note: ἀρχαῖς καὶ ἐξουσίαις ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ τεταγμέναις

pass_b_english: The proconsul kept pressing him. "Swear by Caesar's fortune," he said.

Polycarp answered, "If you imagine in your vanity that I will swear by Caesar's fortune, as you put it, and if you pretend not to know who I am, then listen plainly: I am a Christian. And if you want to learn the teaching of Christianity, give me a day and listen."

Polycarp replied, "You I would have considered worthy of an answer, for we have been taught to give to rulers and authorities appointed by God the honor that is fitting, as long as it does us no harm. But those people I do not consider worthy of making a defense to them."

polish.changed: Clarified who is speaking at each turn, smoothed the sentence order, and removed the awkward 'word of Christianity' phrasing while keeping every claim and qualification.

notes.why: Same Roman authority is called both “proconsul” and “police captain”.

problems.why: The proconsul is named only in section 21; reader may not connect him to 'the proconsul' throughout.
problems.fix: Name him earlier or note the identification.

edits.new: The proconsul Statius Quadratus kept pressing him.

fixed: The proconsul is now named earlier as Statius Quadratus, connecting him to the later mention in section 21.
